commonsFile: File:The Great Clay Mosque in Djenne, Mali.jpg
attribution: Dr. Ondřej Havelka (cestovatel) — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
location: Great Mosque of Djenné, Mopti Region, Mali
alt: The mud-brick Great Mosque of Djenné with its projecting wooden torons and pinnacled towers.
caption: The world's largest mud-brick building, rebuilt in 1907 and re-plastered by the town every year, is the architectural centrepiece of the classic Mali route and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Djenné lies in an area covered by official advice against all travel.

attribution: Ferdinand Reus from Arnhem, Holland — CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Traders and shoppers at the market in front of the Great Mosque of Djenné.
caption: The Monday market fills the square under the mosque with farmers, fishers and Fulani herders from the surrounding delta. It is the reason the classic itinerary is timed to reach Djenné on a Sunday night.

commonsFile: File:Mali, le port de Mopti et ses pinasses (8438033803).jpg
attribution: Jeanne Menjoulet from Paris, France — CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
location: Port of Mopti, Niger inner delta
alt: Wide view of the harbour at Mopti crowded with long wooden pinasses.
caption: Mopti, at the Niger-Bani confluence, is the river port from which pinasses carry salt, millet and passengers across the inner delta. A pinasse trip from here was the traditional way into the delta's villages.

attribution: upyernoz from Haverford, USA — CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: A narrow wooden pirogue on the Niger River in Mali.
caption: Pirogues are the everyday transport and fishing craft of the Niger. On the imagined route they would link Mopti, the delta villages and the ferry crossings.

attribution: upyernoz from Haverford, USA — CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: The Niger riverbank at Ségou with boats and washing on the shore.
caption: Ségou, the former capital of the Bambara kingdom, is the first river town east of Bamako on the road to Djenné. Its riverbank and nearby Kalabougou pottery village were the gentle start of the classic route.

attribution: Ferdinand Reus from Arnhem, Holland — CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: The sandstone cliff of the Bandiagara escarpment rising above the plain.
caption: A 150-km sandstone cliff, up to 500 m high, with Dogon villages on the plateau, at the foot and in older cave dwellings in the rock face. It is the Dogon Country trek that gives the route its adventure, and a UNESCO mixed site.

attribution: Kirua — CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
location: Dogon village below the Bandiagara cliff
alt: Mud-walled granaries with thatched roofs in a Dogon village at the cliff foot.
caption: Dogon villages cluster conical-roofed granaries and flat-roofed houses against the cliff. Walking from village to village with local guides and sleeping on rooftops was the heart of the trip.

attribution: upyernoz from Haverford, USA — CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: A Dogon toguna, a low open men's meeting house with a thick millet-stalk roof and carved posts.
caption: The toguna is the low-roofed meeting place where village elders debate, built low so that no one can stand up in anger. It shows how a Dogon village governs itself.

commonsFile: File:Danse de masques dogon au Mali.jpg
attribution: Fasokan — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Dancers in Dogon masks and fibre costumes performing in a village.
caption: Dogon mask dances mark funerals and the end of mourning and are performed for tourists in some villages. Treating them as paid shows is one of the ethical questions the original route raised.

attribution: Qpallares — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: Wide view of the village of Tireli and its plaza at the foot of the Bandiagara cliff.
caption: Tireli, a village at the foot of the cliff, is one of the traditional trek stops. Dogon communities here have been caught between jihadist groups, the army and inter-communal violence.

attribution: upyernoz from Haverford, USA — CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
alt: The earthen Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu with its buttressed walls and pyramid minaret.
caption: Built in 1327, Djinguereber is one of Timbuktu's three great mosques and a UNESCO site. Timbuktu is the optional extension that is today the least reachable part of the concept.
